topics.title: Classification and nomenclature of halo compounds

learn.hook: PVC water pipes start from vinyl chloride, chloroquine treats malaria, and the halothane once used in operation theatres is a haloalkane. Naming and classifying them is step one.
points: By number of halogen atoms: mono-, di-, tri- or polyhalo compounds.

Compounds with an sp³ C–X bond: alkyl halides (1°, 2° or 3°, by the carbon bearing X), allylic halides (X on an sp³ carbon next to C=C, e.g. CH₂=CH–CH₂Br) and benzylic halides (X on an sp³ carbon attached to a benzene ring, e.g. C₆H₅CH₂Cl).
Compounds with an sp² C–X bond: vinylic halides (X on a C=C carbon, e.g. CH₂=CHCl) and aryl halides (X directly on an aromatic ring, e.g. C₆H₅Cl).
IUPAC names treat halogens as prefixes: CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)CH₃ is 2-chlorobutane, (CH₃)₃CBr is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, CH₂=CHCH₂Br is 3-bromoprop-1-ene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl is (chloromethyl)benzene.

Dihalides: geminal (gem) have both X on the same carbon, e.g. CH₃CHCl₂ (1,1-dichloroethane, ethylidene chloride); vicinal (vic) have X on adjacent carbons, e.g. ClCH₂CH₂Cl (1,2-dichloroethane, ethylene dichloride).

example.q: Give the IUPAC name and classify (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl.
steps: Longest chain containing C–Cl: 3 carbons, Cl on C-1, CH₃ on C-2
Name: 1-chloro-2-methylpropane
The carbon bearing Cl is attached to only one other carbon → primary

learn.reallife: The antimalarial chloroquine and the antiseptic chloroxylenol are halogen compounds, and PVC pipes laid under Indian cities are polymers of chloroethene (vinyl chloride).

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CBr?
quiz.explain: The longest chain is propane with Br and CH₃ both on C-2.
steps: Longest chain through the C–Br carbon: 3 carbons (propane).
Br and CH₃ are both on C-2.
Answer: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane
quiz.mistake: Numbers the chain to give Br the position 1

quiz.q: CH₂=CH–CH₂–Cl is an example of which type of halide?
quiz.explain: Cl is on an sp³ carbon next to a C=C double bond.
steps: Cl is on an sp³ carbon (CH₂) next to the C=C double bond.
That makes it an allylic halide.
Answer: Allylic halide
quiz.mistake: Confuses allylic with vinylic

quiz.q: Which is a vinylic halide?
quiz.explain: In a vinylic halide, the halogen is bonded directly to an sp² carbon of C=C.
steps: A vinylic halide has X on an sp² carbon of C=C.
In CH₂=CHBr, Br is directly on the double-bonded carbon.
Answer: CH₂=CHBr
quiz.mistake: Picks the allylic compound

quiz.q: Which dihalide is a geminal dihalide?
quiz.explain: Both chlorines are on the same carbon (gem = twins).
steps: Geminal (gem) means both halogens on the same carbon.
In CH₃CHCl₂ both Cl are on C-1.
Answer: CH₃CHCl₂
quiz.mistake: Confuses gem with vic

quiz.q: Classify CH₃CH₂CH(Br)CH₃.
quiz.explain: The carbon bearing Br is bonded to two other carbons.
steps: The carbon bearing Br is bonded to two other carbons (CH₂ and CH₃).
So it is a secondary (2°) alkyl halide.
Answer: Secondary (2°) alkyl halide
quiz.mistake: Counts all carbons in the molecule instead of those on the C–X carbon

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of C₆H₅CH₂Cl?
quiz.explain: The Cl is on the CH₂ group attached to the ring, named as a chloromethyl substituent.
steps: Cl is on a CH₂ group attached to the benzene ring.
Named as a substituent: (chloromethyl)benzene.
Answer: (Chloromethyl)benzene
quiz.mistake: Puts the Cl on the ring

quiz.q: In which compound is the C–X carbon sp² hybridised?
quiz.explain: In aryl halides, X is attached to an sp² carbon of the aromatic ring.
steps: In aryl halides X is on a ring carbon, which is sp².
Chlorobenzene is an aryl halide; the others have X on sp³ carbons.
Answer: Chlorobenzene
quiz.mistake: Thinks any compound with a ring or double bond has sp² C–X

quiz.q: Assertion (A): ClCH₂CH₂Cl is a vicinal dihalide. Reason (R): Its two chlorine atoms are on adjacent carbon atoms.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: vic dihalides have halogens on neighbouring carbons, exactly as in 1,2-dichloroethane.
steps: A: ClCH₂CH₂Cl is a vicinal dihalide. True.
R: its two Cl atoms are on adjacent carbons. True.
Adjacent carbons is the meaning of vicinal, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Confuses vicinal with geminal

teach.ask: Gappu gets confused: 'What's the difference between allylic, vinylic and benzylic halides?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Allylic: X on sp³ C next to C=C; vinylic: X on the C=C itself; benzylic: X on sp³ C next to a benzene ring!
teach.nudge: Where exactly is the halogen in each type — on the double-bonded carbon or next to it?

revise.summary: Halo compounds are mono-, di- or polyhalo. sp³ C–X compounds are alkyl (1°, 2°, 3°), allylic and benzylic halides; sp² C–X compounds are vinylic and aryl halides. IUPAC names use halo prefixes; dihalides are geminal (same carbon) or vicinal (adjacent carbons).
focus: Classifying halides by hybridisation and position
traps: Don't call allyl chloride vinylic
Don't classify by the number of halogens when asked 1°/2°/3°; use the carbon bearing X

topics.title: Nature of the C–X bond and physical properties

learn.hook: Chloroform is so dense that it sinks under water in a test tube. Halogens make molecules heavier, more polar and stickier.
points: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar (Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻). From F to I the halogen gets larger, so bond length increases (CH₃F 139 pm → CH₃I 214 pm) and bond enthalpy decreases (452 → 234 kJ mol⁻¹).
Dipole moments: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) > CH₃F (1.847 D) > CH₃Br (1.830 D) > CH₃I (1.636 D); CH₃F is lower than CH₃Cl because of its very short bond.

Boiling points: higher than hydrocarbons of similar mass (polarity, greater mass); RI > RBr > RCl > RF; for isomers, bp decreases with branching (1-bromobutane > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane).
para-Dihalobenzenes have higher melting points than ortho and meta isomers because their symmetry lets them pack better in the crystal lattice.

Bromo, iodo and polychloro compounds are denser than water. Haloalkanes are only slightly soluble in water (the energy needed to break water's hydrogen bonds is not recovered) but dissolve well in organic solvents.

example.q: Arrange 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in decreasing order of boiling point.
steps: All three have the formula C₄H₉Br (same mass)
More branching → more compact shape → smaller surface area → weaker van der Waals forces
1-bromobutane (unbranched) > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (most branched)

learn.reallife: Mothballs used in Indian wardrobes are often 1,4-dichlorobenzene; being the symmetric para isomer, it is a solid that slowly sublimes.

games.title: C–X bond and properties
items: The C–I bond is longer than the C–Cl bond.
C–F has the lowest bond enthalpy among C–X bonds.
C–F is the strongest; C–I is the weakest.
CH₃Cl has a higher dipole moment than CH₃F.
1.860 D versus 1.847 D, because the C–F bond is much shorter.
Haloalkanes are highly soluble in water.
1,4-Dichlorobenzene melts at a higher temperature than 1,2-dichlorobenzene.
The para isomer is more symmetric and packs better.
Polychloro compounds are denser than water.

quiz.q: Which compound has the highest dipole moment?
quiz.explain: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) beats CH₃F (1.847 D) because the C–F bond is very short, reducing charge × distance.
steps: Dipole moment = charge × distance.
C–F is very short, so CH₃F (1.847 D) is below CH₃Cl (1.860 D); Br and I are less polar.
Highest: CH₃Cl.
Answer: CH₃Cl
quiz.mistake: Picks CH₃F because F is most electronegative

quiz.q: How do C–X bond length and bond enthalpy change from C–F to C–I?
options: Bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases
Bond length decreases and bond enthalpy increases
quiz.explain: Larger halogen atoms form longer, weaker bonds with carbon.
steps: From F to I the halogen gets larger.
The C–X bond becomes longer and weaker: length increases, enthalpy decreases.
Answer: Bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases
quiz.mistake: Thinks larger atoms bond more strongly

quiz.q: Which has the highest boiling point?
quiz.explain: Boiling point increases with molar mass and polarisability: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
steps: Boiling point rises with molar mass and polarisability: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
So CH₃I boils highest.
Answer: CH₃I
quiz.mistake: Picks the most electronegative halogen

quiz.q: Why does 2-bromo-2-methylpropane boil at a lower temperature than 1-bromobutane?
options: It has a larger molar mass
Branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface area and van der Waals forces
It has a more polar C–Br bond
quiz.explain: Isomers have equal mass, so the shape decides intermolecular contact.
steps: Isomers have the same mass.
Branching makes the molecule compact, reducing surface area and van der Waals forces, so bp falls.
Answer: Branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface area and van der Waals forces
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of branching on surface area

quiz.q: Why is the melting point of p-dichlorobenzene higher than that of its o- and m-isomers?
options: Its symmetrical shape fits better in the crystal lattice
It has a larger dipole moment
It has a higher molar mass
quiz.explain: The para isomer is symmetric and packs closely, so more energy is needed to melt it.
steps: The para isomer is symmetrical.
It packs better in the crystal, so more energy is needed to melt it.
Answer: Its symmetrical shape fits better in the crystal lattice
quiz.mistake: Thinks the isomers have different masses

quiz.q: Why are haloalkanes only slightly soluble in water even though they are polar?
options: They are less dense than water
Energy released by new attractions with water is less than that needed to break water's hydrogen bonds
quiz.explain: Haloalkanes cannot form hydrogen bonds as strong as those between water molecules.
steps: To dissolve, water's hydrogen bonds must be broken.
Attractions between haloalkane and water release less energy than this, so solubility is low.
Answer: Energy released by new attractions with water is less than that needed to break water's hydrogen bonds
quiz.mistake: Thinks polarity alone guarantees water solubility

quiz.q: Which is denser than water?
quiz.explain: Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives are denser than water.
steps: Bromo, iodo and polychloro compounds are denser than water.
CHCl₃ is polychloro; fluoromethane, chloroethane and methane are lighter.
Answer: Trichloromethane (CHCl₃)
quiz.mistake: Thinks all organic liquids float on water

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Haloalkanes have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass. Reason (R): The C–X bond is polar, and haloalkanes have stronger intermolecular attractions.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Dipole–dipole attractions plus greater polarisability make haloalkane molecules stick together more.
steps: A: haloalkanes boil higher than hydrocarbons of similar mass. True.
R: the polar C–X bond gives stronger intermolecular attractions. True.
Stronger attractions raise bp, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the polar C–X bond to intermolecular forces

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does branching lower the boiling point of bromobutanes even though they have the same mass?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Branching makes molecules compact, cutting surface area and van der Waals forces, so they boil lower!
teach.nudge: You said branching matters. What does it do to the molecule's surface area and intermolecular forces?

revise.summary: The C–X bond is polar; from F to I it lengthens and weakens. CH₃Cl has the largest dipole moment. Haloalkanes boil higher than comparable hydrocarbons; bp rises RF < RCl < RBr < RI and falls with branching. para-Dihalobenzenes melt highest. Haloalkanes are slightly soluble in water.
focus: Polarity, bond length and bond enthalpy trends
Melting point of para isomers; solubility and density
remember: Bromo, iodo, polychloro compounds are denser than water
traps: Don't say CH₃F has the highest dipole moment
Don't say branching raises boiling point

learn.hook: Thionyl chloride is a chemist's favourite for turning alcohols into chlorides. Its by-products simply bubble away as gases, leaving a pure product behind.
points: From alcohols with HX: R–OH + HCl →(ZnCl₂) R–Cl + H₂O. ZnCl₂ is needed for primary and secondary alcohols; tertiary alcohols react with concentrated HCl at room temperature. Reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°.
With phosphorus halides: 3R–OH + PX₃ → 3R–X + H₃PO₃ (PBr₃, PI₃ generated in situ from red P and Br₂/I₂); R–OH + PCl₅ → R–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl.
With thionyl chloride: R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑. Preferred, because both by-products are gases that escape, leaving pure alkyl chloride.
These methods are not used for aryl halides because the C–O bond in phenols has partial double bond character and is hard to break.

Halogen exchange: Finkelstein reaction R–X + NaI →(dry acetone) R–I + NaX (X = Cl, Br); NaCl or NaBr precipitates in acetone, driving the reaction forward. Swarts reaction: CH₃–Br + AgF → CH₃–F + AgBr (also with Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃).

example.q: Why is thionyl chloride preferred for converting ethanol into chloroethane?
steps: C₂H₅OH + SOCl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑
Both by-products are gases and escape
No separation is needed, giving pure chloroethane
example.answer: Because its by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases, leaving the product pure

learn.reallife: India's pharmaceutical industry, the 'pharmacy of the world', uses thionyl chloride and halogen-exchange reactions in many drug syntheses.

quiz.q: What are the by-products when an alcohol reacts with thionyl chloride?
quiz.explain: R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂ + HCl; both are gases.
steps: R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂ + HCl.
Both by-products are gases.
Answer: SO₂ and HCl
quiz.mistake: Gives the PCl₅ by-products

quiz.q: What is the role of anhydrous ZnCl₂ when a primary alcohol reacts with HCl?
options: It acts as a Lewis acid catalyst
quiz.explain: ZnCl₂ coordinates with the OH group, making it a better leaving group.
steps: ZnCl₂ is a Lewis acid.
It coordinates to the OH group, making it a better leaving group for primary and secondary alcohols.
Answer: It acts as a Lewis acid catalyst
quiz.mistake: Thinks ZnCl₂ is a reactant consumed in the reaction

quiz.q: Which reaction converts C₂H₅Br into C₂H₅I?
options: Finkelstein reaction with NaI in dry acetone
quiz.explain: NaI swaps Br for I; NaBr is insoluble in acetone and precipitates.
steps: Finkelstein reaction: R–X + NaI in dry acetone → R–I + NaX.
C₂H₅Br + NaI → C₂H₅I + NaBr.
Answer: Finkelstein reaction with NaI in dry acetone
quiz.mistake: Confuses Finkelstein with Swarts

quiz.q: Why does the Finkelstein reaction go to completion in dry acetone?
options: NaCl or NaBr formed is insoluble in acetone and precipitates out
Acetone reacts with the alkyl halide
quiz.explain: Removing the product salt by precipitation shifts the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier).
steps: NaCl and NaBr are insoluble in dry acetone and precipitate.
Removing a product drives the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier).
Answer: NaCl or NaBr formed is insoluble in acetone and precipitates out
quiz.mistake: Thinks the iodide precipitates

quiz.q: Which reagent is used to prepare alkyl fluorides by the Swarts reaction?
quiz.explain: Heating an alkyl chloride or bromide with a metallic fluoride such as AgF gives the alkyl fluoride.
steps: Swarts reaction: R–Cl or R–Br heated with a metallic fluoride.
AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃ give R–F.
Answer: AgF (or Hg₂F₂, CoF₂, SbF₃)
quiz.mistake: Picks direct fluorination

quiz.q: Which alcohol reacts fastest with concentrated HCl at room temperature without ZnCl₂?
quiz.explain: Tertiary alcohols react readily because they form stable carbocations; reactivity 3° > 2° > 1°.
steps: Reactivity with HCl: 3° > 2° > 1° (more stable carbocation).
Tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol reacts with concentrated HCl at room temperature.
Answer: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary)
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary alcohols are most reactive

quiz.q: Why are aryl halides not prepared by treating phenol with HCl or PCl₅?
options: The C–O bond in phenol has partial double bond character and is difficult to break
quiz.explain: Resonance gives the C–O bond in phenol partial double bond character, so OH cannot be easily replaced.
steps: In phenol the C–O bond has partial double bond character from resonance.
It is hard to break, so OH cannot easily be replaced by Cl.
Answer: The C–O bond in phenol has partial double bond character and is difficult to break
quiz.mistake: Assumes phenols behave like alcohols

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Thionyl chloride is the preferred reagent for preparing alkyl chlorides from alcohols. Reason (R): Both by-products of the reaction are gases that escape easily.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Gaseous SO₂ and HCl leave the reaction, so the alkyl chloride obtained is pure.
steps: A: thionyl chloride is the preferred reagent. True.
R: both by-products are gases that escape. True.
Gases escaping leave pure product, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the gaseous by-products to purity

teach.ask: Gappu needs alkyl iodide: 'How can I swap a bromine for an iodine in an alkyl bromide?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Finkelstein: NaI in dry acetone, and the NaBr precipitates, pushing the swap forward!
teach.nudge: Which reagent and solvent, and why does the reaction go to completion?

revise.summary: Haloalkanes are made from alcohols with HX (ZnCl₂ for 1° and 2°), PX₃, PCl₅ or SOCl₂ (best, as SO₂ and HCl escape). Aryl halides cannot be made this way. Halogen exchange uses the Finkelstein reaction (NaI in dry acetone → R–I) and the Swarts reaction (AgF etc. → R–F).
focus: Reagents for converting alcohols to haloalkanes
Why phenols don't give aryl halides this way
remember: Finkelstein: R–X + NaI → R–I + NaX (dry acetone)
traps: Don't use Finkelstein for fluorides; that is Swarts
Don't forget ZnCl₂ for primary and secondary alcohols with HCl

learn.hook: You can't chlorinate benzene the way you'd chlorinate methane; it needs a Lewis acid helper, or a clever detour through a diazonium salt.
points: Electrophilic substitution: benzene + Cl₂ (or Br₂) with a Lewis acid catalyst (Fe or anhydrous FeCl₃/FeBr₃) in the dark gives chlorobenzene (or bromobenzene). Methylbenzene gives a mixture of ortho and para isomers, which can be separated (the para isomer has a higher melting point).
Iodination is reversible and needs an oxidising agent (HNO₃ or HIO₄) to remove the HI formed. Fluorination is too violent to control, so fluoroarenes are not made this way.
Sandmeyer reaction: an arenediazonium salt (from aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K) is treated with CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr, replacing –N₂⁺ by Cl or Br: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + CuCl → C₆H₅Cl + N₂.
Iodobenzene is made simply by shaking the diazonium salt with potassium iodide: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + KI → C₆H₅I + KCl + N₂.

example.q: How would you prepare iodobenzene from aniline?
steps: Diazotise: aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K → benzenediazonium chloride
Add aqueous KI
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + KI → C₆H₅I + KCl + N₂↑
example.answer: Diazotisation followed by treatment with KI

learn.reallife: Chlorobenzene from plants in Gujarat's chemical clusters is a starting material for pesticides and dyes.

games.title: Benzene to bromobenzene
items: Take dry benzene in the dark
Add anhydrous FeBr₃ (or Fe filings) as Lewis acid

quiz.q: What is the role of anhydrous FeCl₃ in the chlorination of benzene?
options: It is a Lewis acid that generates the Cl⁺ electrophile
quiz.explain: FeCl₃ polarises Cl₂, producing Cl⁺ (as FeCl₄⁻ forms), which attacks the ring.
steps: FeCl₃ is a Lewis acid that polarises Cl₂.
It generates the Cl⁺ electrophile (forming FeCl₄⁻), which attacks the ring.
Answer: It is a Lewis acid that generates the Cl⁺ electrophile
quiz.mistake: Thinks FeCl₃ is a source of chlorine atoms by itself

quiz.q: Which reagent converts benzenediazonium chloride into chlorobenzene in the Sandmeyer reaction?
quiz.explain: Cuprous chloride replaces the diazonium group by Cl, releasing N₂.
steps: Sandmeyer reaction: diazonium salt + CuCl/HCl.
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + CuCl → C₆H₅Cl + N₂.
Answer: CuCl in HCl
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the iodide method

quiz.q: How is iodobenzene prepared from benzenediazonium chloride?
options: By shaking it with potassium iodide solution
By heating with CuI and HCl only
By direct reaction with I₂ and FeCl₃
quiz.explain: KI readily replaces the diazonium group by iodine without needing a copper catalyst.
steps: Iodobenzene needs no copper catalyst.
Shaking the diazonium salt with KI gives C₆H₅I + KCl + N₂.
Answer: By shaking it with potassium iodide solution
quiz.mistake: Applies Sandmeyer conditions unnecessarily

quiz.q: Why is an oxidising agent like HNO₃ needed for direct iodination of benzene?
options: It acts as a Lewis acid
Iodination is reversible; the oxidising agent removes the HI formed
Iodine is not reactive at all
quiz.explain: HI is a strong reducing agent that would reverse the reaction; oxidising it drives iodination forward.
steps: Iodination is reversible because HI is a strong reducing agent.
An oxidising agent (HNO₃ or HIO₄) removes HI and drives the reaction forward.
Answer: Iodination is reversible; the oxidising agent removes the HI formed
quiz.mistake: Thinks HNO₃ is a catalyst like FeCl₃

quiz.q: Why are fluoroarenes not made by direct fluorination of benzene?
options: The reaction with fluorine is too violent to control
Fluorine does not react with benzene
quiz.explain: Fluorine is so reactive that direct reaction cannot be controlled.
steps: Fluorine is extremely reactive.
Its reaction with benzene is too violent to control.
Answer: The reaction with fluorine is too violent to control
quiz.mistake: Thinks fluorine is unreactive

quiz.q: What is formed when methylbenzene (toluene) is chlorinated with Cl₂ and FeCl₃ in the dark?
quiz.explain: The methyl group is ortho/para directing; in the dark with a Lewis acid, substitution occurs on the ring.
steps: The methyl group is ortho/para directing.
In the dark with FeCl₃ the ring is chlorinated, giving 1-chloro-2-methyl- and 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene.
Answer: A mixture of 1-chloro-2-methylbenzene and 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene
quiz.mistake: Confuses ring substitution with side-chain substitution in light

quiz.q: At what temperature range is benzenediazonium chloride prepared from aniline?
quiz.explain: Diazonium salts are unstable and must be made and used in the cold (0–5 °C).
steps: Diazonium salts are unstable and decompose when warm.
They are made in the cold, at 273–278 K (0–5 °C).
Answer: 273–278 K
quiz.mistake: Assumes room temperature is fine

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The ortho and para isomers formed on chlorinating toluene can be separated easily. Reason (R): The para isomer has a much higher melting point than the ortho isomer.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because of the large difference in melting points, the para isomer can be crystallised out.
steps: A: ortho and para chlorotoluenes can be separated easily. True.
R: the para isomer has a much higher melting point. True.
The para isomer crystallises out, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link melting point difference to separation

teach.ask: Gappu wants iodobenzene: 'Why can't I just add iodine to benzene? What's the better way?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Direct iodination is reversible, so I'll diazotise aniline and add KI for iodobenzene. Smart!
teach.nudge: Why is direct iodination tricky, and which salt do you convert first?

revise.summary: Haloarenes are made by electrophilic substitution of arenes with Cl₂ or Br₂ and a Lewis acid (FeCl₃) in the dark; iodination needs an oxidising agent and fluorination is too violent. From diazonium salts (made at 273–278 K), CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr give the halide (Sandmeyer) and KI gives iodobenzene.
focus: Electrophilic halogenation and the role of FeCl₃
Why iodination and fluorination are special
traps: Don't say direct iodination works without an oxidising agent
Don't use UV light for ring chlorination; that substitutes the side chain

topics.title: Nucleophilic substitution: products and ambident nucleophiles

learn.hook: A haloalkane is like a kabaddi raider with a weak hold: a nucleophile tags the carbon and the halide is pushed out. Swap the nucleophile and you get a whole family of products.
points: In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile (electron-rich species) attacks the partially positive carbon of C–X and the halide leaves: Nu⁻ + R–X → R–Nu + X⁻.

Products: OH⁻ (aq KOH) → alcohol; R′O⁻ → ether; I⁻ → alkyl iodide; NH₃ → amine; KCN → alkyl cyanide (nitrile); AgCN → isocyanide; KNO₂ → alkyl nitrite; AgNO₂ → nitroalkane; R′COOAg → ester; LiAlH₄ → hydrocarbon.

Ambident nucleophiles can attack through two different atoms. Cyanide: KCN is ionic, giving free CN⁻ that attacks through carbon (C–C bond is more stable), forming R–CN. AgCN is mainly covalent, so only nitrogen's lone pair is available, forming R–NC.
Nitrite: KNO₂ attacks through oxygen to give alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O; AgNO₂ attacks through nitrogen to give nitroalkane R–NO₂.
Reaction with KCN is useful for increasing the carbon chain by one carbon.

topics.title: SN2 and SN1 mechanisms and reactivity

learn.hook: Two routes, one goal: SN2 is a single swift tackle from behind; SN1 waits for the halide to leave first. Which route a molecule takes depends on its crowding.
points: SN2 (substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular): one step; the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to X (backside attack) as X leaves; the transition state has carbon partly bonded to both. Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (second order). Configuration is inverted (Walden inversion). Example: CH₃Cl + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Cl⁻.
SN2 reactivity: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°, because bulky groups hinder the backside approach (steric hindrance).

SN1 (unimolecular): two steps — slow ionisation of R–X to a carbocation (rate-determining), then fast attack by the nucleophile. Rate = k[RX] (first order). Favoured in polar protic solvents (water, alcohol, acetic acid). Example: (CH₃)₃CBr + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH + Br⁻.
SN1 reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1°, following carbocation stability. Allylic and benzylic halides are very reactive in SN1 because their carbocations are stabilised by resonance.
For the same alkyl group, reactivity of the halide in both mechanisms: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (weaker C–X bond, better leaving group).

example.q: Arrange CH₃Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr and (CH₃)₃CBr in order of increasing SN2 reactivity, and in order of increasing SN1 reactivity.
steps: SN2 is slowed by crowding: (CH₃)₃CBr < (CH₃)₂CHBr < CH₃Br
SN1 depends on carbocation stability: CH₃Br < (CH₃)₂CHBr < (CH₃)₃CBr

topics.title: Stereochemistry: optical activity, chirality and configuration

learn.hook: Your left and right hands are mirror images that never superimpose. Many molecules are 'handed' too, and they twist polarised light in opposite directions.
points: Optically active compounds rotate the plane of plane-polarised light (measured in a polarimeter): dextrorotatory (d or +) to the right, laevorotatory (l or −) to the left.

A carbon bonded to four different groups is an asymmetric carbon (stereocentre); a molecule that is not superimposable on its mirror image is chiral. Butan-2-ol and 2-chlorobutane are chiral; propan-2-ol and 2-chloropropane are achiral.
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. They have identical physical properties (mp, bp, solubility) except the direction of rotation of plane-polarised light.

A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers and shows zero rotation (external compensation); it is written dl or (±). Converting an enantiomer into a racemic mixture is racemisation.

Retention: the spatial arrangement around the stereocentre is preserved. SN2 gives inversion of configuration; SN1 gives mostly racemisation, because the planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.

example.q: Optically active 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed by aqueous KOH via (i) SN2 and (ii) SN1. What is the stereochemistry of butan-2-ol in each case?
steps: (i) SN2: backside attack → inverted configuration, still optically active
(ii) SN1: planar carbocation → attack from both faces
Equal amounts of both enantiomers → racemic mixture, optically inactive
example.answer: SN2 gives inversion; SN1 gives racemisation

learn.hook: Heat 2-bromopentane with alcoholic KOH and two alkenes form, but one wins by a big margin. Zaitsev's rule predicts the winner.
points: Dehydrohalogenation (β-elimination): a haloalkane with a β-hydrogen, heated with alcoholic KOH, loses H and X from adjacent carbons to form an alkene.
Zaitsev (Saytzeff) rule: the preferred alkene is the one with more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons. E.g. 2-bromopentane gives pent-2-ene (81%) rather than pent-1-ene (19%).

Substitution vs elimination: a strong, bulky base favours elimination; primary halides prefer SN2; secondary give SN2 or elimination depending on the base/nucleophile; tertiary give SN1 or elimination depending on carbocation stability and alkene substitution.

Grignard reagent: R–X + Mg →(dry ether) R–MgX. The C–Mg bond is highly polar, so R behaves as a carbanion and reacts with any proton source: RMgX + H₂O → R–H + Mg(OH)X. Hence it must be made under anhydrous conditions. (Victor Grignard, Nobel Prize 1912.)
Wurtz reaction: 2R–X + 2Na →(dry ether) R–R + 2NaX, doubling the alkyl group.

learn.hook: Boil chlorobenzene with aqueous NaOH and almost nothing happens. Industry had to use 623 K and 300 atmospheres to make phenol from it — the Dow process.
points: Haloarenes are much less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophiles because: (i) resonance gives the C–X bond partial double bond character; (ii) the sp² carbon holds the bond more tightly (C–Cl 169 pm in chlorobenzene vs 177 pm in CH₃Cl); (iii) the phenyl cation is not resonance stabilised, so SN1 is ruled out; (iv) the electron-rich ring repels nucleophiles and blocks backside attack.
Dow process: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm gives sodium phenoxide, which is acidified to phenol.

Electron-withdrawing groups like –NO₂ at ortho and para positions make substitution much easier (1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene, then 2,4-dinitro, then 2,4,6-trinitro react under progressively milder conditions); a meta –NO₂ has no such effect.

Electrophilic substitution: the halogen is deactivating (–I effect) but ortho/para directing (+R effect). Chlorination, nitration, sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts alkylation/acylation of chlorobenzene give mainly the para product with some ortho.
Wurtz–Fittig: Ar–X + R–X + 2Na → Ar–R + 2NaX (dry ether). Fittig: 2Ar–X + 2Na → Ar–Ar + 2NaX, e.g. diphenyl from chlorobenzene.

topics.title: Polyhalogen compounds: dichloromethane, chloroform and iodoform

learn.hook: Chloroform was once the anaesthetic of choice in operating rooms. Then doctors noticed something deadly could form from it if bottles were left in the light.
points: Dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂): used as a solvent (paint remover), aerosol propellant, process solvent in drug manufacture and for metal cleaning and finishing. It harms the central nervous system: low exposure can slightly impair hearing and vision; higher levels cause dizziness, nausea and tingling or numbness in fingers and toes; on the skin it causes intense burning, and it can burn the cornea.

Trichloromethane (chloroform, CHCl₃): solvent for fats, alkaloids and iodine; used to make the refrigerant R-22; once a general anaesthetic, now replaced by safer ones. Breathing its vapour depresses the central nervous system; chronic exposure can damage the liver and kidneys.

In air and light, chloroform is slowly oxidised to the extremely poisonous gas phosgene: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ →(light) 2COCl₂ + 2HCl. So it is stored in closed, dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim to keep out air.

Triiodomethane (iodoform, CHI₃) was used as an antiseptic; its action is due to the free iodine it releases, not iodoform itself. Because of its objectionable smell it has been replaced by other iodine-based preparations.
Lab safety: handle these volatile liquids only in a fume hood, with gloves and goggles, and never sniff them directly.

example.answer: To prevent its oxidation to poisonous phosgene

learn.reallife: Industrial safety rules under India's Factories Act require proper ventilation where solvents like dichloromethane are used, for example in paint-stripping and pharma units.

topics.title: CCl₄, freons and DDT: uses and environmental effects

learn.hook: The Montreal Protocol, which India signed, phased out CFCs to heal the ozone hole. The same chlorine chemistry that made freons useful made them dangerous up in the stratosphere.
points: Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄): used to make refrigerants, aerosol propellants and CFCs, in pharmaceutical manufacture and as a solvent; earlier used as a cleaning fluid, spot remover and fire extinguisher. Exposure can cause liver cancer, nerve damage, dizziness and nausea. Released into air, it rises to the stratosphere and depletes the ozone layer.

Freons are chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) of methane and ethane: stable, unreactive, non-toxic, non-corrosive and easily liquefied. Freon-12 (CCl₂F₂) is the most common, made from CCl₄ by the Swarts reaction; used in refrigeration, air conditioning and aerosols.

In the stratosphere, UV light breaks CFCs into chlorine radicals that start chain reactions destroying ozone, letting more harmful UV reach Earth (risk of skin cancer, eye disease and weakened immunity).

DDT (p,p′-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) was the first chlorinated organic insecticide. It was first made in 1873; its insecticidal power was discovered by Paul Müller in 1939 (Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1948). It was widely used against mosquitoes spreading malaria and lice carrying typhus.

Problems with DDT: insects developed resistance; it is highly toxic to fish; it is chemically stable and fat-soluble, so it is not metabolised quickly, gets stored in fatty tissues and builds up along food chains. It was banned in the USA in 1973.

learn.reallife: Under the Montreal Protocol, India completed its CFC phase-out ahead of the Protocol's 2010 deadline and is now phasing out HCFCs used in air conditioners; DDT use in India is restricted to public-health vector control.
